Interstate Commerce. Trade and economic transactions between and across the states of the United States, a domain explicitly placed under federal authority by the Commerce Clause of the Constitution. The power to regulate interstate commerce became one of the most important and expansive federal powers, allowing Congress to address economic matters spanning state lines. This constitutional authority has been the basis for major legislation and judicial decisions that shaped American federalism and expanded federal power. The Commerce Clause in Article I, Section Eight grants Congress power "to regulate Commerce with foreign Nations, and among the several States, and with the Indian Tribes"—one of the most expansively interpreted clauses in the Constitution. It was intended to prevent states from enacting protectionist policies that would balkanize the national economy and harm interstate trade. The Framers had witnessed how economic warfare between states threatened the union under the Articles of Confederation. Gibbons v. Ogden in eighteen twenty-four established that interstate commerce included more than just goods. It encompassed navigation, transportation, and commercial activity affecting interstate trade. Chief Justice Marshall rejected the idea that commerce power was narrowly limited. Wickard v. Filburn in nineteen forty-two dramatically expanded federal power by holding that even local wheat production—consumed on the farmer's own farm—affecting national grain markets could be regulated. This allowed federal control of agricultural production. Interstate commerce authority was used to justify civil rights legislation. Heart of Atlanta Motel v. United States in nineteen sixty-four upheld the Civil Rights Act of nineteen sixty-four as a valid exercise of the commerce power because motels affect interstate commerce and segregation burdens it. The Commerce Clause provides the constitutional basis for federal regulation of railroads, airlines, telecommunications, environmental protection, labor standards, and countless industries spanning state boundaries. This makes it the foundation for most modern federal regulatory authority. Constitutional interpretation has evolved dramatically—the clause's scope has expanded from narrow commercial regulation in the early eighteen hundreds to encompassing broad economic and social policy from the nineteen hundreds onward. Some argue it has expanded so much that limits are now purely political, not constitutional.
